summary: Describes the transport of syslog messages over UDP on IPv4 or IPv6. Implementations of the syslog protocol are required to support this mapping so they can interoperate. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Syslog is how programs send log messages to a central collector. This RFC describes sending them over UDP, the simple connectionless protocol, which is what most existing systems already do. It also sets out plainly what UDP cannot guarantee.

questions: how big can a syslog udp message be
subtitle: How syslog messages travel over UDP, and what that costs in reliability and security.

tldr.problem: Syslog needs one transport that every implementation supports, and the one in wide use carries messages over UDP, which has no delivery guarantee.
tldr.mechanism: Each datagram carries exactly one syslog message, sent to the well-known UDP port 514. Receivers must accept messages of at least 480 octets over IPv4 and 1180 octets over IPv6.
tldr.outcome: The transport is simple and cheap, but messages can be lost, reordered, forged or read in transit. The RFC says the TLS transport should be used instead except on networks provisioned for it.

today: RFC 5426 is a Proposed Standard from March 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the UDP transport mapping for the syslog protocol defined in RFC 5424, and it points at the TLS transport mapping in RFC 5425 as the safer alternative outside managed networks.

sections.title: Why a UDP Transport for Syslog
sections.content:
Informational RFC 3164 describes the syslog protocol as it was observed in existing implementations, covering both the format of syslog messages and a UDP transport. A Standards-Track syslog protocol was later defined in RFC 5424, which specifies a layered architecture that provides for support of any number of transport layer mappings for transmitting syslog messages. This document describes the UDP transport mapping for the syslog protocol, usable over both IPv4 and IPv6.

The syslog protocol layered architecture provides for support of any number of transport mappings, but for interoperability purposes, syslog protocol implementers are required to support this transport mapping. Network administrators and architects should be aware of the significant reliability and security issues of this transport, which stem from the use of UDP. They are documented in this specification. However, this transport is lightweight and is built upon the existing popular use of UDP for syslog.
sections.plainLanguage: Syslog can travel over many transports, but everyone has to support this one so that senders and collectors from different suppliers can talk to each other. The RFC is careful to say that UDP is the least safe of the available options.

sections.title: One Message Per Datagram
sections.content: Each syslog UDP datagram must contain only one syslog message, which may be complete or truncated. The message must be formatted and truncated according to RFC 5424, and no additional data may be present in the datagram payload.
sections.plainLanguage: One datagram, one message. If the message is too long it is cut short, and nothing else may share the datagram.

sections.title: Message Size Limits
sections.content:
This transport mapping supports transmission of syslog messages up to 65535 octets minus the UDP header length, which stems from the maximum supported UDP size of 65535 octets in RFC 768. For IPv4, the maximum payload size is 65535 octets minus the UDP header and minus the IP header, because IPv4 has a 16-bit length field that also includes the header length.

IPv4 syslog receivers must be able to receive datagrams with message sizes up to and including 480 octets, and IPv6 syslog receivers up to and including 1180 octets. All syslog receivers should be able to receive datagrams with message sizes of up to and including 2048 octets, and the ability to receive larger messages is encouraged.

The minimum required message size support was determined from the minimum MTU size that Internet hosts are required to support, 576 octets for IPv4 and 1280 octets for IPv6. Datagrams that conform to these limits have the greatest chance of being delivered because they do not require fragmentation. It is recommended that syslog senders restrict message sizes so that IP datagrams do not exceed the smallest MTU of the network in use, which avoids datagram fragmentation and possible issues surrounding fragmentation such as incorrect MTU discovery.

Fragmentation can be undesirable because it increases the risk of the message being lost due to the loss of just one datagram fragment. Syslog has no acknowledgement facility, and therefore there is no effective way to handle retransmission. This makes it impossible for syslog to use packetization layer path MTU discovery. When the network MTU is not known in advance, the safest assumption is to restrict messages to 480 octets for IPv4 and 1180 octets for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Small messages travel best, because a big one has to be split into pieces and a lost piece loses the whole message. With no acknowledgement there is no way to ask for the missing piece, so the safe rule is to keep messages to 480 octets over IPv4 and 1180 over IPv6.

sections.title: Ports, Source Address and Checksums
sections.content:
Syslog receivers must support accepting syslog datagrams on the well-known UDP port 514, but may be configurable to listen on a different port. Syslog senders must support sending message datagrams to the UDP port 514, but may be configurable to send messages to a different port. Syslog senders may use any source UDP port for transmitting messages.

The source IP address of the UDP datagrams should not be interpreted as the identifier for the host that originated the syslog message, because the entity sending the message could be merely a relay. The syslog message itself contains the identifier of the originator of the message.

Each UDP/IP datagram sent by the transport layer must completely adhere to the structure specified in the UDP RFC and either the IPv4 or IPv6 specification, depending on which protocol is used. Syslog senders must not disable UDP checksums, and IPv4 syslog senders should use them. IPv6 mandates the use of UDP checksums. Syslog receivers must not disable UDP checksum checks; IPv4 syslog receivers should check UDP checksums and should accept a syslog message with a zero checksum.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages go to port 514 unless configured otherwise, and the sending port can be anything. The address the packet came from is not proof of who wrote the message, because a relay may have forwarded it, so the message itself carries the sender's name. Checksums must stay on.

sections.title: What UDP Cannot Promise
sections.content:
UDP is an unreliable, low-overhead protocol, and this section discusses the reliability issues inherent in it that implementers and users should be aware of. This transport mapping does not provide any mechanism to detect and correct loss of datagrams. Datagrams can be lost in transit due to congestion, corruption, or any other intermittent network problem, and IP fragmentation exacerbates this problem because the loss of a single fragment results in the entire message being discarded.

The UDP/IP datagrams can get corrupted in transit due to software, hardware, or network errors. The transport specifies use of UDP checksums to enable corruption detection in addition to the checksums used in IP and Layer 2 protocols. However, checksums do not guarantee corruption detection, and this transport mapping does not provide for message acknowledgement or retransmission.

Because syslog can generate unlimited amounts of data, transferring this data over UDP is generally problematic, because UDP lacks congestion control mechanisms. Congestion control mechanisms that respond to congestion by reducing traffic rates and establish a degree of fairness between flows that share the same path are vital to the stable operation of the Internet. This is why the syslog TLS transport is required to implement and recommended for general use. The only environments where the syslog UDP transport may be used as an alternative to the TLS transport are managed networks, where the network path has been explicitly provisioned for UDP syslog traffic through traffic engineering mechanisms such as rate limiting or capacity reservations. In all other environments, the TLS transport should be used.

The IP transport used by UDP does not guarantee that the sequence of datagram delivery will match the order in which the datagrams were sent. The time stamp contained within each syslog message can serve as a rough guide in establishing sequence order, but it will not help when multiple messages were generated during the same time slot, the sender could not generate a time stamp, or the messages came from different hosts whose clocks were not synchronized. The order of syslog message arrival via this transport should not be used as an authoritative guide in establishing an absolute or relative sequence of events on the syslog sender hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things go wrong with UDP: messages disappear, messages arrive out of order, and nothing slows the sender down when the network is busy. That last one is why the RFC says to use the TLS transport unless the network has been deliberately set up to carry syslog traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using this specification on an unsecured network is not recommended. Several syslog security considerations are discussed in RFC 5424, and this section focuses on those specific to the syslog transport over UDP. Some of the issues raised here can be mitigated through the use of IPsec.

This transport mapping does not provide for strong sender authentication. The receiver will not be able to ascertain that the message was indeed sent from the reported sender, or whether the packet was sent from another device, and an inappropriately configured machine can send messages representing itself as another machine. It also provides no protection against message forgery: an attacker can transmit syslog messages, either from the machine the messages are purportedly sent from or from any other machine.

An attacker can hide the true nature of an attack amidst many other messages. For example, an attacker can start generating forged messages indicating a problem on some machine, which gets the attention of the system administrators, who then spend their time investigating the alleged problem, during which the attacker could compromise a different machine or a different process on the same machine. An attacker can also generate false messages to give untrue indications of the status of systems: the attacker stops a critical process, which generates a notification of exit, and then generates a forged notification that the process had been restarted.

This transport mapping does not provide confidentiality of the messages in transit. If syslog messages are in clear text, this is how they will be transferred. Passing clear-text, human-readable messages is usually a benefit to administrators, but an attacker could observe the contents and use what they learn to compromise a machine. It is recommended that no sensitive information be transmitted via this transport mapping, or that transmission of such information be restricted to properly secured networks.

Message forgery and observation can be combined into a replay attack. An attacker could record a set of messages indicating normal activity of a machine, and later remove that machine from the network and replay the messages with new time stamps, so that the administrators find nothing unusual.

The loss of one or more syslog messages can have security consequences, because administrators could be unaware of a developing and potentially serious problem, and messages could also be intercepted and discarded by an attacker as a way to hide unauthorized activities. This transport mapping does not mandate prioritization of syslog messages, either on the wire or when processed on the receiving host, based on their severity. Unless some prioritization is implemented by the sender, the receiver and the network, the receiver or network devices could get overwhelmed with low-severity messages and be forced to discard potentially high-severity messages. Finally, an attacker could overwhelm a receiver by sending more messages than the infrastructure or the device could handle, so implementers should try to minimize this threat, for example by optionally restricting reception to a set of known source IP addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone on the network path can read the messages, write fake ones, or replay old ones, and the receiver has no way to tell. A lost message can hide a real problem. The RFC's advice is not to send sensitive information this way and to limit which addresses may send.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: This transport uses UDP port 514 for syslog, as recorded in the IANA port-numbers registry. No new registration is needed for this document, because the well-known syslog port already exists in that registry.
sections.plainLanguage: No new registration is needed; the well-known syslog port already exists in the IANA registry.

viz.caption: WHAT THE UDP TRANSPORT DOES NOT PROTECT AGAINST

items.title: No sender authentication
items.text: The receiver cannot tell that the message really came from the host named in it.

items.title: No protection against forgery
items.text: Anyone can send messages that look as though your machines sent them.

items.title: No confidentiality
items.text: Messages travel in clear text, so anyone on the path can read them.

items.title: Replay
items.text: Recorded messages can be sent again later with new time stamps.

items.title: Unreliable delivery
items.text: Messages can vanish, and an attacker can hide activity by discarding them.

items.title: Denial of service
items.text: A flood of messages can overwhelm the receiver.
